author: Mauro Cazzaniga, Florence Jaumotte, Longji Li, Giovanni Melina, Augustus J. Panton, Carlo Pizzinelli, Emma J. Rockall, Marina Mendes Tavares (IMF)
title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
central_scenario_summary: AI is a major productivity shock exposing almost 40 percent of global employment (60 percent in advanced economies); unlike past automation it reaches high-wage cognitive work, with roughly half of exposed jobs at risk of displacement and half complemented. In a UK-calibrated task model with a 5.5pp labor-share decline, labor income inequality rises if AI strongly complements high earners, and capital income and wealth inequality rise in all scenarios; if productivity gains are large (output +16 percent, gains mostly within 10 years), incomes rise across most of the distribution. Policy — property rights over AI, redistribution, safety nets, retraining — shapes the final distributional outcome.

quotes.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is set to profoundly change the global economy, with some commentators seeing it as akin to a new industrial revolution.
Almost 40 percent of global employment is exposed to AI, with advanced economies at greater risk but also better poised to exploit AI benefits

capability_pace.notes: Treats AI as a broad general-purpose technology wave hitting cognitive occupations; no superintelligence or full-automation scenario.

quotes.text: potential AI complementarity is positively correlated with income
with strong complementarity, high-wage earners might experience a disproportionate increase in their earnings, thereby intensifying labor income inequality

expertise_erosion.notes: Two-sided: displacement risk now extends to higher-wage earners (which would erode premia), but the note's emphasized scenario has AI complementing high-income professionals, raising their premia. Scored 0 for the emphasized high-complementarity case; the low-complementarity case would instead compress top labor incomes.

quotes.text: output increases by 16 percent between steady states, and total factor productivity increases by almost 4 percent. These gains happen primarily in the first 10 years of the transition.
In advanced economies, about 60 percent of jobs are exposed to AI, due to prevalence of cognitive-task-oriented jobs.

productivity_breadth.notes: Sizable but conventional gains (roughly +1.5pp annual productivity growth for a decade in the optimistic scenario), concentrated in exposed cognitive occupations; not economy-transforming explosive growth.

quotes.text: AI promises to increase productivity while threatening to replace humans in some jobs and to complement them in others.
A new measure of potential AI complementarity suggests that, of these, about half may be negatively affected by AI, while the rest could benefit from enhanced productivity through AI integration.

substitution.notes: Explicitly mixed: displacement and complementarity channels are modeled jointly; which dominates varies by occupation and scenario.

quotes.text: A rise in aggregate productivity of the economy could however strengthen overall economic demand, potentially creating more job opportunities for most workers in a ripple effect.
higher growth and labor demand could more than compensate for the partial replacement of labor tasks by AI, and incomes could increase along most of the income distribution

demand_absorption.notes: Historical-pattern absorption: productivity gains raise demand for all factors, offsetting displacement if gains are large enough — conditional, not guaranteed.

quotes.text: College-educated workers are better prepared to move from jobs at risk of displacement to high-complementarity jobs; older workers may be more vulnerable to the AI-driven transformation.
For all economies, social safety nets and retraining for AI-susceptible workers are crucial to ensure inclusivity.

mobility_adjustment.notes: Assumes historical mobility patterns (UK/Brazil transition evidence): reallocation happens but is uneven — easier for the college-educated and young, harder for older and less-educated workers; policy support needed.

quotes.text: Unlike labor income inequality, capital income and wealth inequality always increase with AI adoption
Countries' choices regarding the definition of AI property rights, as well as redistributive and other fiscal policies, will ultimately shape its impact on income and wealth distribution.

rent_concentration.notes: Surplus flows significantly to capital owners (higher capital returns accruing to high earners) in every scenario, but the note stresses contested/policy-dependent outcomes rather than winner-take-most firm rents.

quotes.text: These gains happen primarily in the first 10 years of the transition.

timeline_years.notes: Model transition gains concentrated in the first 10 years after adoption; advanced economies affected sooner than EMDEs.

inequality_prediction.score: Labor income inequality may increase if AI strongly complements high-income workers (their earnings rise more than proportionally), while capital income and wealth inequality increase in all scenarios because capital returns rise and assets are concentrated at the top; however, if productivity gains are large enough, income levels rise for most workers (from +2 percent at the bottom to +14 percent at the top in the model), and property-rights and redistributive policy choices ultimately shape the distributional outcome.

quotes.text: Labor income inequality may increase if the complementarity between AI and high-income workers is strong, while capital returns will increase wealth inequality.
Growing AI adoption has the potential to exacerbate cross-country and within-country inequality.
